Methods. We analyzed a dataset of 232 sunspots observed by the HMI instrument, which includes both photospheric and line-of-sight magnetic field measurements. We calculated the rate at which the sunspot areas decreased and correlated this with the strengths of their magnetic fields. 

Results. We discovered a correlation between the rate at which sunspot areas decrease and the strengths of their magnetic fields. However, this correlation only holds true when analyzing sunspots at the time of their maximum areas. When analyzing sunspots throughout their entire lifetimes, we found no connection between their magnetic field strengths and the rate at which their areas decrease. 

Conclusion. We conclude that the decrease in sunspot areas is not caused by a decrease in their magnetic field strengths. Instead, we believe this process is driven by the emergence of new sunspots due to the continuous flow of emerging flux. We also found that the rate at which sunspots decrease is correlated with their initial areas of penetration, which suggests that the decay of sunspots is a self-regulating process. Additionally, we found that the decay rates of sunspots are similar to the emergence rate of new magnetic flux. However, we cannot rule out the possibility of a decrease in the magnetic field strength as a contributing factor to the decay of sunspots. Further research is needed to clarify this relationship. 

Looking ahead. We believe that the observed correlation between sunspot areas and the emergence of new magnetic flux provides valuable insights into the solar cycle. However, we also need more precise data on the emergence of these sunspot groups to better understand this relationship.

Historically, object counting has been a difficult challenge for deep learning models, largely due to the variability in the size, shape, and distribution of objects within an image. Our proposed solution involves a neural network that learns to count objects using a supervised learning approach. By utilizing a convolutional network, we can efficiently extract relevant features from images. These features are then passed through a series of fully connected layers, culminating in a final fully connected layer that yields the object count. During training, we optimize the network's parameters to minimize the discrepancy between the predicted object count and ground truth values. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model excels at object counting, outperforming other deep learning models on standard benchmark datasets.
